title: Sparse neural networks often match or exceed dense models on hard samples at certain sparsity levels
content: Across extensive experiments on CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and CIFAR-10 using standard architectures (ResNet18/34, VGG16/19) and a broad set of unstructured sparsification methods (Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) with the Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) distribution, Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP), Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP), Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) using one-shot magnitude pruning at initialization, and One-shot Magnitude Pruning (OMP) after full dense training), sparse neural networks trained on challenging samples (intrinsically difficult examples selected by Error L2 Norm (EL2N) scores, images with common corruptions such as Gaussian noise and blurring, or adversarially perturbed inputs via Projected Gradient Descent (PGD)) often achieve test accuracy that matches or surpasses the corresponding dense models at particular overall sparsity ratios in the 10%–90% range. This behavior is observed for clean test accuracy and, in adversarial training regimes, for adversarial accuracy (accuracy on perturbed test data) as well.

title: Sparse neural networks provide larger accuracy gains under limited training data
content: When training data are scarce (where the data ratio, the fraction of the challenging subset used for training, is reduced from the full set; examined values include 0.5 and 0.3), sparse neural networks—notably Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) using the Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) distribution, and Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP) using connection sensitivity pruning before training—tend to outperform dense counterparts more markedly than in the full-data regime, with the advantage being most pronounced at higher overall sparsity levels (e.g., 70%–90% sparsity) in the reported experiments.

title: Sparse neural networks improve adversarial robustness while retaining clean accuracy at high sparsity
content: Under adversarial training with Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), with training objective $\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}}\max_{\|\delta\|_{p}\le\varepsilon}\mathcal{L}(f(x+\delta;\theta),y)$ (evaluation used 20-step PGD with maximum perturbation $\varepsilon=8/255$ and step size 2/255), sparse models at high sparsity (e.g., 90% overall sparsity) achieve comparable clean test accuracy and superior adversarial test accuracy compared to dense models on the examined benchmarks (VGG16 on CIFAR-10 and ResNet18 on CIFAR-100). This trend holds at both full and reduced data volumes (e.g., data ratio 0.5) tested in the paper.

title: Layer-wise density allocation (higher shallow-layer density) correlates with better sparse-model performance
content: Sparse methods that allocate higher relative density (proportion of non-zero weights) to early (shallower) layers—for example, Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) allocations used with Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) and the density patterns observed for Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP)—tend to yield higher test accuracy on hard-sample training than uniform per-layer pruning. Empirically, layer-wise density profiles with richer shallow-layer connectivity correlate with improved performance across training on EL2N-selected samples, corrupted images with common corruptions, and adversarial training scenarios (using PGD).

title: Effect of pre-trained initialization: pre-training can compensate for low shallow-layer density; LTH masks may be suboptimal for hard samples
content: Methods that derive sparse topologies from pre-trained dense models (e.g., One-shot Magnitude Pruning (OMP) after full dense training, and the one-shot variant of Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) using pruning at initialization) can tolerate sparser shallow layers because pre-trained weights have already encoded low-level features; however, LTH in the studied setup (one-shot pruning at initialization with rewinding to t=0) sometimes exhibits degraded performance when trained on hard samples (EL2N-selected or corrupted), indicating that masks produced from dense pre-training are not universally optimal for hard-sample regimes. Thus, whether a sparse method starts from a pre-trained dense model or from scratch materially affects performance on hard samples and interacts with the layer-wise density allocation.

title: Trade-offs in computational cost: SET and SNIP reduce FLOPs and parameters while matching or improving accuracy; LTH/OMP incur extra FLOPs from pre-training
content: Dynamic-sparse training methods that form sparse topologies before or early during training (e.g., Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) with Erdős–Rényi–Kernel (ERK) distribution, and Single-shot Network Pruning (SNIP)) achieve the dual benefit of test accuracy improvement and reduced training floating-point operations (FLOPs) and parameter counts in the evaluated hard-sample regimes (EL2N-selected, corrupted, adversarial); by contrast, dense-to-sparse procedures that require obtaining a fully trained dense model (e.g., Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) with one-shot pruning at initialization and One-shot Magnitude Pruning (OMP) after full training) incur additional training FLOPs due to dense pre-training, even though the resulting sparse models may have fewer parameters.

title: SNN advantage varies with corruption severity and can diminish at extreme corruption levels
content: When training on inputs corrupted by common visible degradations (e.g., Gaussian noise, blurring, impulse noise) at a training data ratio of 0.3 (using 30% of the corrupted subset), the relative benefit of sparse neural networks (SNNs) over dense models grows as corruption severity increases from low to moderate levels (severity 2 to severity 4 on the 1–6 scale), but at extreme corruption severity (severity 6) the relative improvement shrinks or disappears for some sparse methods.
